overview: The Maurya dynasty, founded by Chandragupta around 321 BCE, ruled one of South Asia's largest ancient empires from Pataliputra. Its many regions and communities did not live identically. Ashoka's third-century BCE inscriptions let us hear a ruler explaining what he wanted officers and families to do; archaeological objects reveal other kinds of work. Royal orders are evidence of plans and values, not proof that every village obeyed them.

periods.title: A new imperial centre
periods.summary: Chandragupta and Bindusara expanded power from the Ganges plain over a wide and diverse realm.

periods.title: Ashoka's reign
periods.summary: After war in Kalinga, Ashoka publicised moral and administrative policies in inscriptions.

periods.title: After Ashoka
periods.summary: The dynasty continued for decades before the last Mauryan ruler was overthrown.

items.text: Chandragupta's realm stretched from Bengal west toward Afghanistan by about 303 BCE, and Bindusara extended control into parts of central and southern India. A map of this huge domain cannot tell us that every district was governed in the same way. People in its farming districts, ports and towns had their own languages and local ties.

The Greek diplomat Megasthenes described Pataliputra, the capital, as a city guarded by a wooden wall with many gates and towers. His reported counts are a visitor's account, not a measurement surviving on the ground. Timber construction and a capital full of officials show why an empire needed more than battlefield victories to function.

Before and during the Mauryan age, trade and gift exchange linked South Asian kingdoms and republics. Roads, towns, coins and merchant guilds grew in importance over the wider sixth-to-third-century period. A family selling grain or craft goods lived inside this network even if it never saw an emperor. These were regional changes, not inventions credited to one Mauryan ruler.

Ashoka's own thirteenth rock edict says the conquest of Kalinga brought killing, deportation and separation of relatives. He presents remorse and argues that conquest by moral teaching is better. Those are powerful words from the winner of a war; the inscription also reminds us that people who survived had to rebuild their ordinary lives.

One edict mentions the small ceremonies families performed when a child was born, someone married, a person was ill or a journey began. Ashoka criticised some of these practices and recommended care toward servants, teachers and living creatures. The scolding tone is useful evidence: families had rituals of their own, even when the court wanted to reform them.

Ashoka said he arranged medical treatment for people and animals, imported useful plants where needed, and had wells and trees placed along roads. We can learn what he wanted travellers and patients to have. His inscription does not tell us how many wells actually worked, whether every village received care or whether a treatment cured anyone.

The court also wanted officials to travel rather than stay at their desks. An edict directs several classes of officers to make inspection tours every five years and to speak about respect for parents, generosity and restraint in spending. Governing a far-flung realm meant sending messages and people across long distances; the text gives an order, not a surviving trip diary.

sections.title: Words in stone and work in the hand

items.text: A small surviving fragment of Ashoka's sixth pillar edict is carved on burnished sandstone. The British Museum dates the fragment to the middle of the third century BCE. Pillars could bring the ruler's message into a public place, but this broken piece reminds us that even stone records survive unevenly. It preserves part of a text, not an entire imperial archive.

A sample of inscriptional Prakrit in modern Roman transliteration is “Devānāmpriya Priyadarśī Rāja”, the royal style meaning roughly “King, beloved of the gods, who looks graciously upon all.” This is the scholarly edition's rendering of Ashoka's title, not a picture of Brahmi letters cut into a particular stone. Different inscription sites used scripts and languages suited to their audiences.

A carved steatite ring stone from northern India shows goddesses and water plants. The Met dates it broadly from the third to late second century BCE, so it may not belong to a single ruler's reign. Gold foil found with similar discs suggests such stones could have been jewellers' moulds. Someone's skilled hands may have turned the carved design into a very different shining object.

sections.title: A sacred place that kept changing

items.text: At Sanchi, Ashoka's patronage is associated with a stone pillar and an early brick stupa. Later rulers enlarged the mound, added stone casing and railings, and eventually built the famous carved gateways. This is a splendid example of a place outliving an empire: a visitor can see centuries of additions, not one building completed under Ashoka.

ending.text: Around 185 BCE, the Mauryan general Pushyamitra Shunga killed the last Mauryan king and took power. The Shunga realm did not simply inherit the whole empire. Buddhist sites such as Sanchi continued to be enlarged under later dynasties, and the many peoples of the former Mauryan lands continued their lives beyond the fall of one ruling family.
